dispositions.method: The automatic families first printed in 1803 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 1,416 items printed somewhere; by the finder's count, with papers that have two or three catalogue numbers taken as one, 2 reach 10 papers, 15 reach 9, 33 reach 8 and 41 reach 7). The same script was run with year 1802 over the 1803 pages (items_from_1802.json: 189 items, 5 in 9 papers, 10 in 8 and 6 in 7). Every item in 7 or more papers was read, and every item in 5 or 6 papers that a comparison of about 220 words of its text with every page put in more papers was checked. A sweep of the year for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 7 or more papers found short items that the reuse families had not joined, and those were counted too. Every item that might reach 7 was counted again by its own words, in both transcriptions, and with phrase searches over all 3,250 pages of 1803, reading every hit.
dispositions.selection_rule: The one admission rule (R-01), as for 1776, 1800, 1804, 1805, 1806, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single printed item in 9 or more newspapers is admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; items are counted one by one; a sub-story may have fewer papers when its parent reaches 7. No year-specific threshold: items of 1803 reach 7, 8, 9 and 10 papers. 10 to 12 papers are in print in any three weeks from January to April, 10 to mid-June, and 8 or 9 from late June to December, so from July an item in 9 papers was printed by every paper that survives for its weeks. Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01). Nothing is held back for its subject.
dispositions.paper_counting: 1803 has 17 catalogue series, which are 12 papers (C-04): the Alexandria Advertiser and Commercial Intelligencer (sn84024011, to 16 September) and the Alexandria Daily Advertiser (sn84024012, from 19 September, continuing its numbering); the Kentucky Gazette (sn82014782 on 4 and 11 January, then sn84038147); the United States Oracle of Portsmouth (sn83025545, to 15 October) and the Oracle Post (sn84023351, from 25 October), its country edition, which continues its volume numbering; Jenks' Portland Gazette under three catalogue numbers (sn83016072, sn83021505, sn83016081). Each counts once. No 1803 issue has a corrected date.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item, six items of 1803 reach 9 or 10 papers: the President's message of 22 December 1802 on the deposit at New Orleans (9, by its printings of 1803), the Spanish minister's letter of 10 March (9), the French chargé d'affaires' letter of 11 March (9), the Spanish minister's letter of 19 April (10), Mr. Gascoigne's letter of 8 March brought by the ship Mercury (10, within three New York reports) and the President's message of 17 October (9). Twenty-three items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen and twenty-one are not. Every other item is in 6 papers or fewer by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains the acts of the second session of the Seventh Congress (and of the first session of the Eighth) through their enacting formula and the list of acts, the Secretary of the Treasury's reports of December 1802 and October 1803 through their common opening, and paragraphs of the House's daily proceedings. Each text was counted by its own words. No act reaches 7 papers by its own title: the laws were printed by authority in the National Intelligencer, the New Hampshire Gazette, the Republican Ledger, the Kentucky Gazette and the Rhode-Island Republican (5 papers), and a few also in the Recorder or the Oracle (6). The act of 31 October to take possession of Louisiana is in 6 papers; the Senate's bill for it, printed a week earlier, in 7 (not chosen; as 1809 kept a Senate bill apart from its act).
counted_item_by_item.A sweep for short items: The reuse families join printings that share long passages, and the finder takes its candidates from them, so short items printed in many papers can be missed. This review also swept every page of 1803 for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 7 or more papers, and counted every item it surfaced by its own words. It found Colonel Despard's speech, Mr. Gascoigne's letter, the National Intelligencer's paragraph on the treaty of cession and the convention for the occupation of Hanover among the admitted items, and several items in 7 or 8 papers that are listed as not chosen. The earlier reviews did not run such a sweep (a note for the audit).
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item printed within different reports or in different translations counts as one (C-02): Mr. Gascoigne's letter within three New York reports of the ship Mercury's arrival (10 papers; the reports themselves share no other text), Colonel Despard's speech within three London accounts of his execution (8), the French note of 13 May and the convention for the occupation of Hanover in two translations each, the Rotterdam paragraph on the Louisiana expedition with the Kentucky Gazette's shorter form, the Dublin letter with the New Hampshire Gazette's printing from its second sentence, and Mr. Monroe's letter with the Oracle's own heading.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: A paper that printed an item twice has two printings (C-08): the National Intelligencer printed the Senate's resolutions on 80,000 militia as moved and as adopted, the Spanish minister's letter of 10 March again on 30 March ('We, therefore, re-insert it'), Colonel Despard's speech in two accounts, and the treaty and both conventions again with the President's proclamation on 2 November.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote, summarise or reci: Not counted (C-07): the House's resolution of 7 January quoted in an essay on the purchase of Louisiana (National Intelligencer, 3 October), in a review of the session (Oracle, 26 March) and in a satirical paragraph (Alexandria Advertiser, 24 February); the Senate's resolutions quoted in the same essay; the Spanish minister's letter quoted in an essay (Alexandria Advertiser, 24 March); the Boston report of Mr. Eaton's arrival from Tunis quoted in the National Intelligencer's answer to it and in the Kentucky Gazette; the British declaration of May summarised by the Berkeley and Jefferson Intelligencer and the Kentucky Gazette; the Spanish royal order on Louisiana summarised by the New Hampshire Gazette and the Republican Ledger; the President's circular letter to the governors paraphrased in the Governor of New Hampshire's speech; the act to take possession of Louisiana named in the House's proceedings.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs of the proceedings: As in the 1800 and 1804 reviews (X-1800-08, X-1804-04), each paragraph of the reports of the House's and the Senate's proceedings is counted as an item by its own words; the day's proceedings as a whole stay a digest. Three such paragraphs reach the band: the House's resolution of 7 January (8, admitted), the Senate's resolutions on 80,000 militia (8, admitted) and Mr. Ross's resolutions (7), and in the House Mr. Rutledge's resolution on duties on arms imported for the militia (7). The others the finder put in 7 or more are in 6 or fewer by their own words.
counted_item_by_item.This year's printings: A reviewed year's group holds only that year's printings (C-11). The President's message of 22 December 1802 is admitted by its nine printings of January 1803 (the National Intelligencer printed it in December 1802); the President's annual message of 15 December 1802 is in 6 papers in 1803 and the Secretary of the Treasury's report of December 1802 in 7, most of their printings being of December 1802.
